content: In June 1992, in response to Resolution 46/182, the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) was established as the primary mechanism for inter-agency coordination in humanitarian assistance during complex and major emergencies. This initiative operates under the leadership of the United Nations Emergency Relief Coordinator (ERC). The IASC is composed of the heads or designated representatives of United Nations operational agencies, including the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the World Food Programme (WFP), the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-HABITAT), the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA), and the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Additionally, standing invitations are extended to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the Special Rapporteur on the Human Rights of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), and the World Bank. In 2006, the ERC, in collaboration with the IASC, initiated the Humanitarian Reform process to enhance the effectiveness of humanitarian responses by improving predictability, accountability, responsibility, and partnerships. As part of these efforts, the cluster approach was introduced and adopted. Clusters are groups of humanitarian organizations, both United Nations and non-United Nations entities, organized by sector (e.g., health, logistics, nutrition, protection, shelter, education, water and sanitation/hygiene, early recovery, food security, camp management, and emergency telecommunications). These clusters are designated by the IASC and have clearly defined responsibilities for coordination. Agencies not formally part of the cluster system, such as the ICRC, often coordinate with it in most situations. Each sector or area of activity has a designated Global Cluster Lead, which provides surge capacity, technical expertise, stockpiles, tools, and best practices, including monitoring and evaluation. For example, WHO is the Global Cluster Lead for Health, UNHCR leads the Protection cluster, and UNICEF leads the Education cluster. At the country level, the Cluster Lead Agency is designated by the Resident Coordinator and/or Humanitarian Coordinator. Each cluster is led by a Cluster Coordinator, who is responsible for coordination and facilitating the cluster’s work. In the health sector, cluster coordination often involves co-chairing by WHO and a representative of the national government. The Humanitarian Coordinator, as the highest representative of the international humanitarian response, ensures the coordination and effectiveness of response efforts. The Humanitarian Coordinator also establishes and leads the Humanitarian Country Team, a strategic and operational decision-making body that includes representatives from the United Nations, IOM, international NGOs, and the Red Cross/Red Crescent Movement. This team is responsible for agreeing on common strategies, including which clusters to establish and which organizations will lead them. Agencies designated as Cluster Leads are expected to represent both their respective clusters and their organizations. Palliative care clinicians and teams can contribute to humanitarian responses in several ways. They may volunteer with local governmental organizations or international/local NGOs to assist during domestic humanitarian emergencies and crises. Clinicians already working in a country affected by a sudden emergency may also play a role. However, ad hoc volunteering and deployment without proper preparation can lead to uncoordinated or substandard care. Therefore, palliative care clinicians interested in participating in humanitarian responses should contact their National Disaster Management Office (NDMO) and familiarize themselves with the cluster approach. They should be prepared to deploy when requested by the NDMO or health cluster and respect the sovereign role of the state in determining the type, location, and timing of assistance. Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) are groups of health professionals (e.g., doctors, nurses, paramedics) that provide medical care domestically and internationally during humanitarian emergencies and crises. EMTs may be composed of professionals from governments, NGOs, academic institutions, the military, and international humanitarian organizations such as the Red Cross/Red Crescent. WHO and its partners have established minimum standards for EMTs to ensure they are adequately trained, prepared, and self-sufficient, so as not to burden the national systems of affected states. Historically, EMTs were primarily prepared to provide surgical and trauma care. However, the Ebola outbreak in West Africa highlighted the need for medical intensive care, leading to an expansion of EMT roles. WHO classifies EMTs into three types: Type 1 provides outpatient emergency care, Type 2 provides inpatient surgical emergency care, and Type 3 provides complex inpatient referral surgical care, including intensive care capacity. Specialized care teams, including palliative care clinicians, may be embedded within inpatient settings of hospitals or EMT Types 2 and 3. WHO has developed a Global EMT Registry to verify that EMTs meet minimum standards and to facilitate coordinated deployment. Type 1 EMTs should include at least one physician and one nurse with basic palliative care training (35–70 hours). Type 2 and 3 EMTs, which are likely to care for critically ill or dying patients, should include at least one physician with intermediate-level palliative care training (two to six weeks). Additionally, all anesthetists and anesthesia technicians should have basic palliative care training. Palliative care specialists joining EMTs should be prepared to address the needs of individuals affected by mass casualty events, infectious disease outbreaks, and famine. They should also undergo basic training in humanitarian emergency response. International conventions mandate access to essential controlled medicines. The primary objective of international drug control conventions is to ensure the availability of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances for medical and scientific purposes while preventing their diversion for illicit use. The United Nations Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs of 1961 and the Convention on Psychotropic Substances of 1971 established a dual-purpose control system to ensure the availability of controlled substances for medical purposes while preventing their misuse. Essential opioid analgesics, such as morphine, are indispensable for pain relief and must be adequately provided. Inadequate access to opioid analgesia is inconsistent with Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which includes the right to medical care, encompassing palliative care. Barriers to opioid use reported by countries include a lack of prescriber training, fear of addiction or dependence, financial constraints, sourcing or importing difficulties, burdensome regulatory frameworks, fear of diversion, and fear of prosecution for prescribing. These barriers should be addressed by EMTs and national governments. EMT staff should be trained in opioid analgesia and supply chain security. Restrictions on opioid prescribing during humanitarian emergencies should be eliminated in accordance with WHO or other internationally recognized standards. Simplified control measures are in place for the provision of controlled medicines during emergencies, allowing for expedited import and delivery by recognized organizations. These measures are outlined in WHO guidelines for the international provision of controlled medicines for emergency medical care. The Core Humanitarian Standard (CHS) on Quality and Accountability outlines nine commitments to maximize the quality and effectiveness of humanitarian assistance. It promotes accountability to communities and people affected by crises, enabling them to hold humanitarian organizations accountable. The CHS describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action and serves as a voluntary code for organizations to align their internal procedures or as a basis for performance verification.
